analysis.one_liner: Bars lawsuits against food and beverage companies blaming them for weight gain and obesity.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 276-139 in March 2004, but the Senate never voted on it, and it died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: Known as the "cheeseburger bill," this measure would stop people from suing food and beverage manufacturers, sellers, advertisers, and trade associations over weight gain, obesity, or related health conditions in any federal or state court. It would also dismiss lawsuits already in progress when the bill became law. A few claims would survive: suits alleging the company knowingly and willfully broke a law governing how food is made, marketed, or labeled; breach of an express warranty; adulterated food; and actions under the Federal Trade Commission Act or the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. The stated purpose was to leave obesity policy to Congress, state legislatures, and regulators rather than to courts and juries.
analysis.who_benefits: Food and beverage manufacturers, sellers, advertisers, and their trade associations gain, because lawsuits blaming their products for obesity and weight-related health problems would be barred in every state and federal court, including suits already filed. Companies facing obesity-related suits would be freed of the cost and risk of defending them, and the threat of judgments could no longer push them to change how they market high-calorie foods.

how_it_helps.text: It bars new lawsuits and dismisses pending ones against food and beverage makers, sellers, advertisers, and trade associations over injuries tied to weight gain, obesity, or related health conditions.

The shield applies in both federal and state courts and covers a wide range of relief — damages, penalties, restitution, and injunctions — so companies and trade groups would be protected across the board.

It does allow suits alleging a knowing and willful violation of federal or state law, breach of an express warranty, adulterated food, or violations of the Federal Trade Commission Act or the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people who are harmed by the food they buy pay, in two ways: anyone whose obesity-related injury stems from how food was marketed or made loses a major route to compensation, and consumers as a whole lose the leverage that lawsuits provide to hold companies accountable for misleading marketing. The few claims the bill allows require proving a knowing violation of law with detailed pleadings, a much higher bar than the ordinary state-law claims it eliminates.
analysis.who_pays_short: People harmed by unsafe or misleadingly marketed food

drawbacks.text: The bill dismissed pending lawsuits as well as barring new ones, so people who had already filed obesity-related claims would have lost their day in court the moment the bill became law.

It covered suits for damages, penalties, restitution, and injunctive relief alike, so it did not just block large class actions; it also blocked a single person or even a state government entity from suing over obesity-related injury.

Even the preserved exceptions were harder to use: a plaintiff alleging a knowing violation of law had to identify the specific federal and state statutes violated and plead the facts of causation with particularity, and discovery was stayed while a motion to dismiss was pending, raising the cost and difficulty of bringing a case.
Opponents argued the bill stripped state courts and juries of their traditional role in deciding product liability claims, replacing state law with a federal shield for one industry.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a clear, one-sided benefit: it removed a new category of lawsuits, saving the food industry money and sparing companies and trade associations the cost of defending obesity claims. But the cost fell on consumers. State-law product liability suits are one of the few tools individuals have to force companies to answer for deceptive marketing or unsafe products, and the bill would have eliminated that tool for obesity-related harms, including retroactively dismissing cases already in court. The exceptions — knowing violations of law, breach of express warranty, adulterated food — preserved some remedies, but they raised the pleading bar (requiring plaintiffs to specify the statutes violated and facts showing causation) and froze discovery while motions to dismiss were pending, making even the surviving claims harder to bring. An honest supporter would call this a reasonable response to lawsuits that stretched liability beyond its proper purpose; an honest critic would note that it shifted the risk of obesity-related harm from the companies marketing high-calorie foods to the people who eat them, with no offsetting measure — such as stronger nutrition disclosure — addressing the underlying public health problem.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 276-139, but the Senate let it sit on its calendar and never brought it to a vote, and it expired when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced by Rep. Ric Keller of Florida on January 27, 2003 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee.
It gathered 119 cosponsors — 110 Republicans and 9 Democrats.
The Judiciary Committee held a hearing and a markup, ordered the bill reported amended by voice vote, and reported it on March 5, 2004.
The House debated several amendments on March 10, 2004 and passed the bill 276-139, with 221 of 227 Republicans voting yes and 137 of 205 Democrats voting no.
The Senate received the bill on March 11, 2004, read it twice, and placed it on the Senate calendar, where it stayed without any further action through the end of the Congress on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Food and beverage companies and their trade associations got what they wanted in the House but were left exposed to state-law lawsuits when the bill stalled in the Senate; consumers and state courts kept the existing ability to sue over obesity-related harms. Everyone stayed where they were — the bill changed nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers kept the right to sue; food companies stayed exposed

industries.industry: Food, beverage, and restaurant companies and their trade associations
industries.note: The bill gave the industry an across-the-board shield against obesity-related lawsuits, including suits already filed, in every state and federal court. This protected the industry's core business model — selling and heavily marketing high-calorie foods — from the one legal threat that could force changes in how those products are marketed.

The bill eliminated an emerging category of lawsuits, taking away work and the possibility of large recoveries for lawyers who bring civil claims against large companies. That loss lined up with the public interest in keeping a remedy available, since the same suits were the only pressure point the bill removed.

industries.industry: Advertisers and marketers of food and beverages
industries.note: The shield covered advertisers and marketers of food products, insulating them from obesity-related claims, while the exception for knowing violations of laws governing marketing and advertising left some room to sue over deceptive practices.
